$comment: Every number this page draws, tied to the committed blob it came from.
The page's thesis is 'every number is traceable to the repository it came
from'. Until this file existed that was a slogan: the plates and the prose
were checked against EACH OTHER (gate.mjs check 9) and against nothing else,
so two authored strings could agree perfectly and both be false. Three rounds
of audits found exactly that.
A row is a derivation, not a citation. `extractor` is a shell command run
against $BLOB — the file fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at `ref`,
which is a COMMIT SHA, never a branch name. Its stdout must equal `value`
exactly. Nobody has to trust the number; they run the command.
`drawn_on` is where the value appears on this page. build/claims.mjs checks
both directions: every row must re-derive, AND every number a plate draws
must have a row here or an entry in `exempt`. A claims file that only
verified the numbers it happened to list would be the same gate-that-cannot-
fail this project has already shipped twice.

claims.extractor: grep -cE '^ALTER TABLE .* FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' "$BLOB"
claims.note: Anchored to ^ALTER TABLE on purpose. A bare `grep -c 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY'` returns 8, because the file's own header comment explains what FORCE does — the same prose-counting mistake as the row above, in a file where it would have inflated the claim. user_profiles is deliberately excluded from RLS (0002_enable_rls.sql:21-22), so 'every tenant table' is seven, and the README now says seven. ROUND 28: the README sentence this anchored was cut; plate-5-cadence and m-5-cadence draw 'RLS FORCEd on all 7 tables', so the row pins the occurrence that exists. README's only 7 is now 'Seven systems', a different noun, exempted by name rather than licensed by this row.

Counted from the guard in the QUERY, not from a comment about it. The previous row here counted the word IDOR in docstrings and returned 7; four different methods return 7, 8, 9 and 15, so the count of vulnerabilities is an audit finding and belongs in prose. How many services now scope by owner is a property of the code. Round 27: plate-5 left this row's drawn_on — the rebuilt plate draws the six services as six row-pairs, marks rather than a word, and a mark is not a token this gate can read. The README still says six and this row still holds it.

Replaces the 'five of six app-side guards' both cadence plates drew until 2026-08-12, and the two exemptions that carried it. That five was not reproducible, and four methods disagreed about it. A literal grep of `if (context?.userId)` finds it in ALL SIX services — 2, 9, 5, 6, 8 and 7 occurrences. Classifying each guard conditional-vs-unconditional makes AttachmentService the only all-conditional service, so five services have a MIX: a different five. Restricting to the by-id path gives 8 unguarded sites in CalendarService, which would be a live IDOR and is contradicted by the audit that closed all six. And the retired prose simply asserted it. The house rule is that a number two methods disagree on does not get published, so the count came off the plate and this row derives the statement every one of those methods agrees on. WHAT IT PROVES: each of these six files carries at least one owner guard written as a CONDITION, so the scoping is a branch a caller can fail to take. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: not that every guard inside a service is conditional, not that every by-id path carries one, and not that the guard is sufficient — those are the three readings that produced three different fives, and the plate now claims none of them. The line loses nothing it could support: the app-side guard is skippable, and the database's refusal is not. Deliberately the same six paths as cadence.idor_services and deliberately a different property — that row counts services that scope by owner IN THE QUERY (AND "userId" = $), this one counts services whose app-side guard is a condition. Both are 6; neither licenses the other's sentence. Not expected-zero, and self-controlling in the sense the tree() note in claims.mjs asks for: a typo'd pattern or wrong escaping prints 0, not 6, so this fails in the unflattering direction as well as the flattering one.

benchDot/256, openmp+native against the plain course baseline, derived as a ratio of two committed medians rather than stored. Re-sourced 2026-08-10 from docs/benchmarks/bench_summary.csv to the 20-repetition dot20x pair, for the reason recorded on glyph.axpy128_slowdown: the CSV is the December record on a different machine, and glyph's ENVIRONMENT.md names the 2026-08-02 M1 Pro runs as the reference. This is also the pair glyph's own README calls the figure to cite -- tightest coefficient of variation on record for this kernel, 0.2% and 0.3%. Three artifact-backed readings span 3.504x (CSV), 3.536x (dot20x, 20 reps) and 3.570x (aggregated, 10 reps); the first two round to 3.5 and the third to 3.6, so WHICH artifact is canonical decides the drawn digit. That is the whole argument for retiring the CSV rather than keeping both.

The answer that went against the author, printed on purpose: the same openmp+native flags that win benchDot/256 LOSE benchAxpy/128. Below a size floor, threading costs more than it pays, and the page says so. This read 6.9x until 2026-08-10, sourced to docs/benchmarks/bench_summary.csv. That figure was arithmetically correct and pointed at the wrong machine: bench_summary.csv is the December record, taken on Shrees-MacBook.local, and glyph's own docs/benchmarks/ENVIRONMENT.md retires it in one line -- 'The 2026-08-02 runs on the M1 Pro are the reference. The December runs are history.' For an OpenMP scaling ratio a fanless 4-performance-core machine is a different ceiling, not a noisier reading of the same one, which is why the two baselines agree within 8% while the two parallel numbers differ by 69%. Both glyph ratios now derive from the 2026-08-02 reference machine. They come from two runs on it because only one of them measures axpy: the dot20x pair carries no benchAxpy rows at all.

The three thresholds below are the only numbers section VII draws that describe a DECISION rather than an amount of effort. Lines of code and file counts measure how much was typed; these measure what the app does to a person walking. They are private `let` constants on LiDARService — and round 25 found the sharper fact this note used to soften. It said 'the Settings sliders do not reach them, so a user cannot tune the distance', which reads as a design choice. It is not: SettingsView.swift draws a real Slider bound to @AppStorage('alertDistance'), with an accessibilityValue read aloud, and LiDARService never references UserSettings at all. The control exists, is reachable by a low-vision user, announces its value, and changes nothing. That is a defect in an accessibility app, not a decision, and the page now says so.

The widest ring is the one that says the most about the design: inside 2.0 m the obstacle is drawn on screen and deliberately NOT announced. An aid that narrates every wall is an aid people switch off, so silence here is a feature with a threshold attached, not an omission.

$unpinnable_note: This list held exactly one row — AutoML's '2 approval gates' — filed under
the reason 'the repo is private'. That diagnosis was wrong, and the way it
was wrong matters more than the number.
The count was not merely unverifiable. It was FALSE: the reproducible count
of human-gate stages is four (preprocessing await_approval, feature
engineering await_review, training propose_model and await_review). By
filing it as 'private, therefore unpinnable' this file certified a wrong
number as an acceptable one, and printed a friendly note where it should
have failed. A category that excuses a claim from being checked will,
sooner or later, be where a false claim goes to live.
So there is no such category any more. Plate VI no longer draws a count at
all; it draws the mechanism and says on its face that this is the one
section a reader cannot check. Anything drawn must derive or be exempt.

$attested_note: Facts about the AUTHOR rather than measurements of a repository.
Everything in `claims` is re-derived in CI from a pinned commit, and that is
the page's whole argument. A year of internship work is not in any repository
a reader can clone: the Oracle logs, the Tableau inventory and the compliance
dashboard belong to Miami University. Nor is a competition result.
Those facts are worth putting on the page, and pretending they carry the same
warrant as `422 MB/s` would be exactly the move this document exists to
refuse. So they live here, they are labelled ATTESTED on the plate that draws
them, and claims.mjs prints them separately from the derived set. The reader
is told which numbers they can check and which they are taking on trust.
